documents.title: Generational Rings of Primes: An Orthogonal Composite Stream Sieve

constraints: heap must stay O(pi(sqrt N)) records, not O(N)

nodes.name: Lemma 1: Composite up to N^2 Has a Prime Factor at Most N
nodes.statement: Every composite m with 2 <= m <= N^2 has a prime factor p <= N.
nodes.formal: m = ab,\ 1<a\le b \Rightarrow a^2\le ab=m\le N^2 \Rightarrow a\le N

representation.content: Write m = ab with 1 < a <= b. Then a^2 <= ab = m <= N^2, so a <= N.

sources.heading: 2.1 The Basic Structural Fact
sources.quote: Let \(m\) be composite with \(2 \le m \le N^2\). Then \(m\) has a prime factor \(p \le N\).

nodes.name: Primes up to N Are a Complete Divisor Basis for N^2
nodes.statement: The primes up to N can be treated as a complete divisor basis for all numbers up to N^2.

sources.heading: 1. Introduction
sources.quote: those primes form a complete divisor basis for the entire band up to \(N^2\)
This lemma means that the primes up to N are a complete divisor basis

nodes.name: Naive Layered Trial-Division Extension Is Not Attractive
nodes.statement: Extending primes from N to N^2 by trial division against all primes up to N is correct but not asymptotically attractive for bulk generation.

sources.heading: 1. Introduction
sources.quote: naive application leads to trial division by \(\pi (N)\) primes for roughly \(N^2\) candidates. That is not asymptotically attractive

nodes.name: Represent Composites as Orthogonal Per-Prime Streams and Merge
nodes.statement: Instead of testing candidates, assign every composite to exactly one prime stream (its smallest prime factor) and merge those streams to find the next prime.

sources.heading: 1. Introduction
sources.quote: It is about a different representation: instead of testing candidates, we assign every composite to exactly one prime stream

sources.heading: 1. Introduction
sources.quote: assign every composite to exactly one prime stream

nodes.name: Ownership Convention for Composites
nodes.statement: A composite number m is owned by the prime p if p is the smallest prime factor of m.

sources.heading: 2.4 Orthogonal Streams
sources.quote: A composite number \(m\) is **owned** by the prime \(p\) if \(p\) is the smallest prime factor of \(m\).

nodes.name: Ownership Streams Are Disjoint and Cover All Composites
nodes.statement: If each stream contains exactly the composites owned by its prime, the streams are pairwise disjoint and together cover all composite numbers.

sources.heading: 2.4 Orthogonal Streams
sources.quote: Every composite has exactly one owner. Therefore ... the streams are disjoint and together cover all composite numbers.

nodes.name: Orthogonal Stream of a Prime
nodes.statement: The stream of prime p consists of p times the p-rough numbers from p up, i.e. Theta_p = p * A_p where A_p = {a >= p : gcd(a, P_<p) = 1}.

sources.heading: 2.4 Orthogonal Streams
sources.quote: \Theta_p \;=\; p \cdot A_p, \qquad A_p = \{\, a \ge p : \gcd (a, P_{<p}) = 1 \,\}

nodes.name: NextOwnedComposite Primitive
nodes.statement: NextOwnedComposite(p, x) is the minimum element of Theta_p strictly greater than x.

sources.heading: 3.1 Definition
sources.quote: \text{NextOwnedComposite} (p, x) \;=\; \min\{\, m \in \Theta_p : m > x \,\}

nodes.name: NextOwnedComposite Equals a Wheel Successor
nodes.statement: NextOwnedComposite(p, x) equals p times NextRough(p, max(p-1, floor(x/p))), the least p-rough integer above that threshold.

sources.heading: 3.2 It is exactly a wheel successor
sources.quote: The owned composites are \(pa\) with \(a \in A_p\), and \(pa > x \iff a > \lfloor x/p \rfloor\)
So there is no additional formula to find: the generator is a merge of wheel successor functions

nodes.name: Minimum Element of a Prime's Stream Is Its Square
nodes.statement: The minimum of Theta_p is always p^2, since the least multiplier of p is p itself.

sources.quote: **Corollary.** \(\min \Theta_p = p^2\) — always, not "typically", since the least multiplier is \(p\) itself.

nodes.name: Phase Separation of a Prime's Multipliers
nodes.statement: The multipliers of p split into a prime phase on [p, p^2) where advancing is a single index increment into the known prime array, and a rough phase on [p^2, infinity) where composite multipliers appear.

sources.heading: 3.3 Phase separation
sources.quote: the multipliers of \(p\) split into a **prime phase** \([p, p^2)\) ... and a **rough phase** \([p^2, \infty)\)

nodes.name: The Generator Is Self-Hosting (Causality)
nodes.statement: If all primes less than n are known and n = pa is in the stream of p, then by Bertrand's postulate the next multiplier a' is less than n, so no step ever requires knowledge of an integer beyond what the generator has already output.

sources.heading: 3.4 Causality
sources.quote: the generator is self-hosting, and its own output supplies every multiplier it will ever need, strictly in advance

nodes.name: Conjecture X1: No O(1)-Time Poly-Space NextRough Algorithm
nodes.statement: No algorithm computes NextRough(p, y) in O(1) time and poly(log p, log y) space given only the primes less than p.

interfaces.note: stated as conjecture X1 / theory.md T31, unproved

sources.quote: no algorithm computes \(\text{NextRough} (p,y)\) in O (1) time and \(\mathrm{poly} (\log p, \log y)\) space given only the primes \(< p\)

nodes.name: Algorithm A: Exact Orthogonal Streams
nodes.statement: Algorithm A derives rough multipliers exactly from other streams so every composite is touched exactly once, at the cost of a growing number of simultaneously live streams (~N^0.75).

sources.quote: **Algorithm A** _derives_ the rough multipliers from other streams. Exact: every composite is touched exactly once

nodes.name: Algorithm B: Shared Fixed Wheel Across Primes
nodes.statement: Algorithm B relaxes the multiplier set to a single fixed wheel W shared by every prime above the wheel primes, giving O(1) time and O(1) state per prime at the cost of duplicate composite touches.

sources.quote: **Algorithm B** _relaxes_ the multiplier set to a single fixed wheel \(W = p_1\cdots p_w\) shared by every prime
Past a fixed table boundary, one of two things must happen

nodes.name: placeholder-unused
nodes.statement: unused

sources.heading: n/a
sources.quote: n/a

nodes.name: Algorithm B Is the Recommended Realisation
nodes.statement: Algorithm B is recommended as the practical realisation; Algorithm A is retained as the mathematically pure reference because its one-touch property certifies the partition.

sources.quote: Algorithm B is the recommended realisation. Algorithm A is retained as the mathematically pure reference

nodes.name: Consuming Merge Algorithm with Deferred Activation
nodes.statement: The consuming algorithm maintains a min-heap keyed by each active prime's next claimed composite, an activation cursor that inserts a prime's stream only when the scan reaches p^2, and emits n as prime whenever n is strictly below the heap minimum.

representation.content: H := empty min-heap; P := []; act := 0; n := 2; while generating: activate primes with p^2<=n; if H empty or n<min_key(H) emit n; else drain(H,n); n:=next_candidate(n)

sources.heading: 4.2 Algorithm Description
sources.quote: H   := empty min-heap\nP   := empty list\nact := 0            # activation cursor into P
Exact streams (Algorithm A). next_candidate(n) = n + 1
Shared wheel (Algorithm B). next_candidate(n) steps over W-coprime integers only

nodes.name: Deferred Activation Bounds Heap Size to pi(sqrt n)
nodes.statement: Inserting a prime's stream only at n = p^2 keeps the heap at pi(sqrt n) records forever, with no global limit and no pre-pass.

sources.heading: 4.1 Data Structures
sources.quote: keeps the queue at \(\pi (\sqrt n)\) records forever, with no global limit and no pre-pass

nodes.name: Theorem 1: Correctness of the Consuming Algorithm
nodes.statement: The consuming algorithm emits all primes in increasing order; under exact streams every composite is removed exactly once, by its smallest prime factor.

representation.content: Invariant: after processing all integers < n, heap contains for every active prime p exactly the least element of Theta_p >= n; no key < n.

sources.heading: 4.4 Correctness
sources.quote: The consuming algorithm emits all primes in increasing order; under exact streams every composite is removed exactly once

nodes.name: Exact Streams Have Optimal Event Count
nodes.statement: Under exact streams the algorithm performs exactly N - pi(N) - 1 pops, one per composite, which is optimal.

sources.heading: 4.5 Complexity
sources.quote: Exact streams: exactly \(N - \pi (N) - 1\) pops, one per composite — optimal.

nodes.name: Shared-Wheel Event Count Approximation
nodes.statement: The shared-wheel realisation performs approximately kappa_W * N * (ln ln sqrt N - ln ln p_w) operations, e.g. about 0.46N at w=6, N=10^12, versus the one-touch ideal of about 0.19N, a factor of about 2.4.

sources.heading: 4.5 Complexity
sources.quote: e.g. \(\approx 0.46\,N\) at \(w=6\), \(N=10^{12}\), against the one-touch ideal \(\approx 0.19\,N\) — a factor \(\approx 2.4\)
Shared wheel: ops(N) ≈ ...

nodes.name: Time Complexity of the Consuming Algorithm
nodes.statement: The algorithm runs in O(N log log N) time with a binary heap, or O(events) amortised with a bucket priority queue.

sources.heading: 4.5 Complexity
sources.quote: \(O (\text{events} \cdot \log \pi (\sqrt N)) = O (N \log\log N)\) with a binary heap

nodes.name: Memory Complexity: O(pi(sqrt N)) Records
nodes.statement: Memory is O(pi(sqrt N)) records plus O(W) bytes of wheel table for the shared-wheel realisation; exact streams require about N^0.75 live streams.

sources.heading: 4.5 Complexity
sources.quote: For exact streams the live-stream count is larger, \(S (N) \approx N^{0.75}\); that is the price of exactness.

nodes.name: Tabulating Roughness Is O(1) Time but Not O(1) State
nodes.statement: Tabulating the totative list of P_

sources.quote: past \(p \approx 29\) it exceeds \(10^9\). So this is O (1) time but _not_ O (1) state.

nodes.name: Untabulated Roughness Test Is Superlinear via Jacobsthal Gaps
nodes.statement: Without tabulation, testing roughness costs Theta(pi(p)) trial divisions, and Jacobsthal-type gap bounds mean scan-and-test can be superlinear in p in the worst case.

sources.quote: by Jacobsthal-type bounds the gap to the next rough number can be \(\gg p \log p \log\log\log p / (\log\log p)^2\)

nodes.name: O'Neill's Genuine Sieve (Priority-Queue Multiple Tracking)
nodes.statement: O'Neill's genuine sieve tracks multiples per prime via a priority queue, but the streams are not pre-orthogonalized, so up to omega(n) entries can collide at n.

sources.heading: 5.1 Comparison with Classical Sieves
sources.quote: **Priority-queue multiple tracking** (O'Neill's "genuine sieve"): tracks multiples per prime, but the streams are not pre-orthogonalized
at most one heap entry equals any given value — the distinguishing property

nodes.name: Sieve of Eratosthenes
nodes.statement: The sieve of Eratosthenes requires a marking array proportional to the search range, with orthogonalization only implicit.

sources.heading: 5.1 Comparison with Classical Sieves
sources.quote: **Eratosthenes:** requires a marking array proportional to the search range; orthogonalization is implicit, not per-prime.

nodes.name: Sieve of Atkin
nodes.statement: The Atkin sieve uses quadratic forms and heavy branching, and is conceptually opaque.

sources.heading: 5.1 Comparison with Classical Sieves
sources.quote: **Atkin:** uses quadratic forms and heavy branching; conceptually opaque.

nodes.name: Classical Wheel Sieves
nodes.statement: Wheel sieves precompute residue tables with orthogonalization applied globally rather than per-prime.

sources.heading: 5.1 Comparison with Classical Sieves
sources.quote: **Wheel sieves:** precompute residue tables; orthogonalization is global rather than per-prime.

nodes.name: Shared-Wheel Advance Vectorises Across Streams
nodes.statement: The bucketed shared-wheel advance step (gather plus multiply) vectorises across streams and bucket drains are independent scatter writes; this is an engineering claim to be benchmarked, not a theorem.

sources.heading: 5.2 Control Flow and Vectorisation
sources.quote: This is an engineering claim to be benchmarked, not a theorem.

nodes.name: Exact Realisation Does Not Support Independent Segment Restart
nodes.statement: The exact realisation costs N^0.75 live streams and does not support independent segment restart.

sources.heading: 5.4 Limitations
sources.quote: The exact realisation costs \(N^{0.75}\) live streams and does not support independent segment restart.

nodes.name: Wheeled Realisation Pays a ln ln Duplicate-Touch Overhead
nodes.statement: The wheeled realisation costs a ln ln factor of duplicate touches and a Theta(W) table, but supports exact segment parallelism.

sources.heading: 5.4 Limitations
sources.quote: The wheeled realisation costs a \(\ln\ln\) factor of duplicate touches and a \(\Theta (W)\) table.

nodes.name: Neither Realisation Beats a Highly Optimized Segmented Sieve on Raw Throughput
nodes.statement: Neither the exact nor the wheeled realisation beats a highly optimized segmented sieve on raw single-core throughput; the value is architectural.

sources.heading: 5.4 Limitations
sources.quote: Neither beats a highly optimized segmented sieve on raw single-core throughput. The value is architectural.

nodes.name: Generational Rings of Primes
nodes.statement: Primes are exception points of an expanding periodic lattice; each new prime becomes a generator of the next periodic structure, and the deleted set at each stage is an affine copy of the previous stage.

sources.heading: 5.3 Generational Ring Clarity
sources.quote: primes are the exception points of an expanding periodic lattice; each exception becomes a generator of the next periodic structure

nodes.name: Band Recursion (Square-Root Bands)
nodes.statement: Seeded with 2 and 3, stage p closes the window [p^2, p'^2) where p' is the next prime, certifying all primes in that window.

sources.heading: 2.3 Generational Structure
sources.quote: stage \(p\) closes the window \([p^2, p'^2)\) where \(p'\) is the next prime

nodes.name: Lattice Recursion (Primorial Stages)
nodes.statement: Working modulo primorials, S_{k+1} is formed by tiling the previous lattice S_k p times and deleting one dilated copy of it, where p is the (k+1)-th prime.

sources.heading: 2.3 Generational Structure
sources.quote: tile the previous lattice \(p\) times and delete one **dilated copy of it**

nodes.name: Band and Lattice Recursions Certify the Same Window
nodes.statement: The band recursion and lattice recursion certify primality on the same window: the holes of stage k are prime exactly on [p_{k+1}, p_{k+1}^2), and merely candidates above it.

sources.heading: 2.3 Generational Structure
sources.quote: Both recursions certify primality on the same window: the holes of stage \(k\) are prime exactly on \([p_{k+1}, p_{k+1}^2)\)
